540.title: Hidden from the wise (Luke 10:21–24)
540.hook: Jesus rejoices that simple people understand
540.howItsDone: Many Christians treasure Luke 10:21 as a reminder that faith is open to everyone, and teachers of prayer across traditions often speak of receiving God like a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy sent out two by two, and your line: peace be to this house.

The Gospels show Jesus weeping, sighing, angry at injustice, tired enough to sleep through a storm. They seldom say outright that he was joyful. So these four verses stand out. The seventy have just come back buzzing with stories, and Luke says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit." The Greek verb is stronger than the English: exulting, overjoyed, the same family of words Mary used when she sang that her spirit rejoiced in God. What could make him that happy? Not who you'd expect.

In the King James words: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight." Babes, in Greek nepioi, means little children, infants. Not the experts, not the people with the best schooling or the highest positions. Luke never tells us who the seventy were, only that they went out with no purse and no bag, and they've just seen what many learned people missed. Jesus isn't against learning; Luke opens his Gospel saying he investigated everything carefully. The point is the door you come in by. Some things you don't grasp by being clever. You grasp them the way a child does: by trusting, by receiving, by not pretending you already know. The people who are sure they understand can find the door closed precisely because they're sure. Then Jesus turns to his disciples privately: "Blessed are the eyes which see the things that ye see: For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them." Isaiah, David, all the great names longed to see this, and the ones who got to see it are ordinary people from Galilee. It's a warm reversal, and it fits Luke's whole Gospel: the shepherds before the priests, the widow before the rich, the child set beside him. The ones who receive are the ones who know they need to.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE EYES WHICH SEE THE THINGS THAT YE SEE.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who taught you the most important things, not from a stage but by how they lived: a grandmother who prayed while she cooked, a child who forgave quickly, a coworker with no title who always knew the right thing to do, someone with a disability or a hard life who sees what others miss. Let one face come, and ask what they understood that cleverness couldn't teach. If you pray, give thanks for your unexpected teachers; if you don't, simply honor them.
Nepioi, Greek for little children, infants: Jesus rejoices that what the clever missed has been revealed to little children, ordinary people who simply received it.
Your line: revealed to babes. Some things are received, not figured out. See you tomorrow.

541.title: Who is my neighbor? (Luke 10:25–37)
541.hook: a lawyer's question and a story that asks who acted like a neighbor
541.howItsDone: Hospitals, charities and the emergency-helper laws known as Good Samaritan laws take their name from this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nepioi: what the clever missed, revealed to little children. Your line was revealed to babes.

It starts as a test. A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, stands up: "Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns it back: how do you read the law? The lawyer answers well, joining two lines from Deuteronomy and Leviticus: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus says: "This do, and thou shalt live." But the lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asks one more question, about where the edges are.

"And who is my neighbour?" Where can I stop? Jesus answers with a story. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead." A priest passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, does the same. Readers have guessed why, fear, hurry, worry about touching what might be a corpse, but Luke is silent. Then a Samaritan comes, one of the same people whose village, a chapter ago, would not receive Jesus. "And when he saw him, he had compassion on him," the same words Luke used for Jesus at the widow's gate in Nain. He bandages the wounds, pouring in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal and walks. He leaves two coins, two pence in the King James, with the innkeeper: "Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee." Then Jesus flips the question: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" The lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; some readers think he couldn't bring himself to. He says: "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus: "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted a boundary. He gets a verb. Neighbor isn't a category of people you owe. It's something you become.

`A PRIEST, A LEVITE: THE OTHER SIDE.`
`NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO WAS A NEIGHBOR.`
then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Think about your own road, the commute, the hallway at work, the group chat, and who has been left out, knocked down by bad news, or stuck beside it. Then think of someone from the other side of some line, politics, faith, class, a family feud, hold them in mind without arguing, and picture crossing the road toward them as the Samaritan did, with one small act of mercy. If you pray, hold that person before God; if you don't, simply picture the crossing.

Your line: go and do likewise. Mercy crossed the road. That's day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
542.hook: Martha is busy and cross; Mary sits at his feet; one thing is needed
542.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a short time of quiet prayer or Bible reading before the day's work begins, and in monastic communities, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican, the day is shaped by set hours of prayer between hours of work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, plesion, the one near you: a Samaritan who stopped, and your line, go and do likewise.

Luke tells this story in five verses, straight after the good Samaritan. Yesterday's hero stopped and did something. Today, a guest arrives in a village, and the person doing everything gets a gentle word. A woman named Martha received him into her house: her house, her welcome, her guest. Luke only says there was much serving; it isn't hard to imagine bread to bake and water to carry. Her sister Mary is sitting on the floor, listening. Anyone who has been the one at the sink while others laugh in the next room may recognize Martha.
screen: `ONE AT THE SINK, ONE ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." That's the place of a student; Paul later says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Mary takes that place, one some readers think was usually kept for men, and nobody sends her back to the kitchen. Martha "was cumbered about much serving." Luke's Greek word has the sense of being pulled around, drawn in every direction. Finally she comes in: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me." She doesn't speak to Mary; she goes over her head. The answer is gentle. He says her name twice, the way you do with someone you love: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her." Careful here means full of care, anxious. He doesn't tell Martha to stop cooking or call serving wrong; one story earlier, the Samaritan was all service. What he names is the worry, the many things crowding out the one. Christians read the sisters in more than one way. Some early writers saw two callings, the active life and the quiet life of prayer, and monasteries tried to keep both. Others say every person has a Martha and a Mary inside. And Martha gets her own great moment later: in John's Gospel, she tells Jesus plainly that she believes he is the Christ. Nobody here is the villain. One sister just needed to sit down first.

Before the next thing on your list, sit down the way Mary did, as if someone worth listening to were in the room, and name two or three of the many things pulling at you. Set each one down. If you pray, simply listen without asking for anything; if you don't, listen to the quiet, to your breath, to whatever is actually here.
Martha. The sister who welcomed Jesus into her home and was pulled in every direction by much serving, while Mary sat at his feet and listened.
Your line: one thing is needful. The worry, not the work. Day five hundred forty-two, done.

543.title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–4)
543.hook: Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer
543.howItsDone: Christians say the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home, usually in Matthew's wording; some churches add the closing doxology straight after it, while the Catholic Mass places it after a short prayer by the priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha, pulled in every direction, and Mary at his feet. Your line was one thing is needful.

Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer: at his baptism, all night before choosing the twelve, on the mountain when his face changed. Today he is praying in a certain place, and his friends wait a little way off until he finishes. When he stops, one of them asks a question. Not about miracles, not about the kingdom, not about who's the greatest. Just this: show us how.

In the King James Bible: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John the Baptist had taught his followers to pray; now they want to be taught too. What Jesus gives is short. The King James text of Luke reads much like Matthew's; some modern Bibles print Luke's version shorter still, opening with one word, Father, and then five requests. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Bread for each day. Forgiveness. And protection from the time of trial. Two small differences from Matthew are worth hearing. Luke's bread line is "Give us day by day our daily bread." Day by day: not a stockpile, a habit. And where Matthew says debts, Luke says: "And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." Sins for what we've done, debts for what others owe us; Matthew uses debts for both. One more surprise: the closing line, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, isn't in Luke at all, even in the King James. The King James has it in Matthew. Some churches say it straight after the prayer; in the Catholic Mass it comes a moment later, after another short prayer by the priest. So a prayer said in churches today began as a short answer to a simple request. Teach us.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say Luke's King James lines slowly, one per breath, with long gaps: hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; give us day by day our daily bread; and forgive us our sins, for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us; and lead us not into temptation. If you don't pray, take just one of those requests, bread, forgiveness or protection, and sit with the one that names something you actually need today.
Father. The one word Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer opens with, a disciple's request after watching Jesus pray, answered with just five requests after it.
Your line: teach us. It's a request anyone can still make. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: A friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–13)
544.hook: a friend knocks for bread at midnight and keeps knocking
544.howItsDone: Some Christians bring the same request to God again and again, in personal prayer, in prayer lists kept by churches, and in intercessions during Sunday worship, reading this story as permission to keep asking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disciple said teach us to pray, and the prayer opened with one word: Father.

Straight after the prayer, Jesus tells a story with a very practical problem. It's midnight. A friend has turned up from a journey, tired and hungry, and there's nothing in the house to set before him. Not a loaf. There's one option left: walk down the dark lane to a neighbor's house, where the door is shut and the children are already in bed, and knock loudly enough to be heard.

The man at the door calls out, in the King James Bible: "Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?" From inside comes an answer any parent of small children might give: "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee." But the knocking doesn't stop. Jesus says the neighbor will get up, not because they're friends, but "because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity is the old English word. The Greek is anaideia: shamelessness, a nerve that doesn't care how it looks. Readers differ about whose shamelessness it is. Some hear the knocker's, refusing to give up. Others hear the sleeper's, getting up to avoid the shame of failing a neighbor. Either way, the story isn't saying God is a grumpy neighbor who has to be nagged. It works by contrast: if even a sleepy friend gets up at midnight, how much more will God. Then: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." And Luke ends with a twist of his own. Matthew says the Father gives good things. Luke says: "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" His last word here isn't bread at all, but the Holy Spirit.
screen: `TROUBLE ME NOT: THE DOOR IS SHUT.`
`NOT A GRUMPY GOD: HOW MUCH MORE.`
then, large: `KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you really need that you've stopped asking for because it felt embarrassing, or greedy, or too late, and let it come to mind plainly. If you pray, ask for it in your own words, the way you'd ask a friend, without polishing the request, and then ask again. If you don't pray, simply admit the need to yourself without apologizing for it.

Anaideia, Greek for shamelessness, nerve, which the King James Bible calls importunity: a man knocks on a barred door at midnight for three loaves and keeps knocking, and the story says, how much more will God give.
Your line: shamelessly ask. A shut door isn't the end of this story. That's five hundred forty-four.

545.title: The lamp of the eye (Luke 11:14–36)
545.hook: take heed that the light in you is not darkness
545.howItsDone: Some Christians practice a slow, attentive looking as prayer, with icons in Orthodox churches, with art and nature in many retreat traditions, and with the Ignatian habit of noticing where God was present in the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anaideia: a friend at midnight who kept knocking, and your line, shamelessly ask.

This part of Luke is noisy. Jesus heals a man who couldn't speak, and some in the crowd say he does it by the power of the prince of demons. He answers that a house divided against itself falls. A woman shouts a blessing on his mother. Others demand a sign from heaven. And in the middle of all that heat, he stops and talks about something quiet: a lamp in a room, and the light that comes in through your eyes.

First, the lamp. Nobody lights one and hides it under a bushel; you set it on a stand so whoever walks in can see. Then, in the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness." Single sounds odd to us. The Greek word, haplous, means simple, whole, undivided: an eye that sees clearly because it isn't split between ten things. And in Jesus' world, a good eye and an evil eye were also ways of talking about money and people. A generous person had a good eye; a stingy, envious one had an evil eye. Proverbs says: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor." Paul later uses a word from the same family as haplous for generosity. So the saying is about more than eyesight. How you look at people fills you up. Look at the world with envy or suspicion, and the darkness gets inside. Look with a clear, generous eye, and you fill with light. Then a short, sharp warning: "Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness." You can think you're seeing clearly and be wrong. In a chapter full of people who looked straight at a healing and saw the devil, that line lands hard. The crowd wanted a sign from the sky. He points them back to their own eyes.
screen: `A GOOD EYE IS A GENEROUS EYE.`
then, large: `THE LIGHT OF THE BODY IS THE EYE.`

segments.voice: Find one thing in front of you or out of a window, a tree, a face in a photo, the light on a wall, a cup, and let your eyes rest on it alone, bringing them back whenever your attention splits. Look at it generously, the way you'd look at something you love, without judging it or wanting anything from it. If you pray, give thanks for what you see; if not, notice what happens inside you as you look.
Haplous, Greek for single, simple, whole: Jesus says the eye is the body's light, and a clear, generous eye like that fills you with light, while an envious one lets the darkness in.
Your line: keep the light in. A clear eye is a generous one. Day five hundred forty-five, done.

546.title: Clean on the outside (Luke 11:37–54)
546.hook: he eats with Pharisees and challenges religion that's all surface
546.howItsDone: Some Christians pair outward practices, like grace before meals, tithing or fasting, with an inward examination of conscience, and the season of Lent joins fasting with prayer and almsgiving, the giving this passage names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haplous, the single, generous eye, and your line: keep the light in.

A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner, and Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once. The Pharisees in this scene care about holiness at the table itself: washing, tithing, cups and dishes. So when the guest sits straight down without washing, the host is startled. The King James Bible says he "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner." And Jesus, at someone else's table, answers the look on his face.

"Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness." Ravening means grabbing, greed. It's a sharp thing to say at dinner, and Luke doesn't soften it. Then a riddle: "did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?" God made the cup's inside as well as its outside; you can't polish one and ignore the other. His answer to how is surprising: give alms from what's within, and everything is clean. Generosity cleans the inside of the cup. Then he names their careful tithing, a tenth of even mint and rue from the herb garden, and says they pass over justice and the love of God. But listen to the end of the sentence: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." He doesn't throw out the small faithful habits. He says do both. This is the language of Israel's own prophets, speaking to their own people. Micah asked what the Lord requires, and answered: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. It's an argument inside a family, and any church can hear it about itself. And so a week on the road closes: wisdom given to little ones, a Samaritan who stopped, Martha and Mary, a short prayer, a friend knocking at midnight, a lamp in the eye, and now a cup that needs washing on both sides.

segments.voice: Pick up a cup or bowl near you, or picture one, and look into it; then turn your attention inward, to what sits inside you that nobody else can see: a grudge, a little greed, a story you tell yourself about someone. Don't scrub at it; just name it honestly, and think of one generous thing you could give from the inside out: time, money, a kind word you've been holding back. If you pray, offer that inside place to God as it is; if you don't, simply let it be named.
Alms. Jesus's answer to how the inside of the cup gets clean: give from what's within to the poor, and everything is made clean.
Your line: the inside too. Generosity reaches where polish can't. A week on the road, closed.
